extracted.intended_audience: researchers and psychometricians validating personality/humor inventories (e.g., psychologists, personality researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Psychometric evaluation and short-form construction of the State‑Trait Cheerfulness Inventory (STCI‑T) English version, including item analyses, factor analyses (EFA/CFA), reliability assessment, and criteria for deriving a 60‑item standard form. Intended to guide scale validation and item reduction decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal consistency (Cronbach Alpha)
rubrics_metrics.description: Report Cronbach's alpha (α) for total scores and facets (e.g., CH α = 0.89; SE α = 0.87; BM α = 0.94).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret α for totals and facets; high α for totals supports reliability. Facet-level α values may be lower; when facets show low α (e.g., SE facets), caution is advised. The article recommends relying on total scores for most purposes and not using facets for diagnostic purposes if their reliabilities are low.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrected item‑to‑total correlation (CITC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute corrected item‑to‑total correlations for each item and report mean CITC per facet/scale (e.g., CH mean CITC ranged 0.34–0.66).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use CITC to flag weak items; the authors treat CITC > 0.30 as a minimal acceptable threshold and note items below this as problematic (several items did not reach >0.30). CITC informs item selection for short form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive statistics: means, SD, skewness, kurtosis (normality checks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Report item/facet/scale mean, standard deviation, skewness and kurtosis and check for deviations from normal distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use skewness and kurtosis to judge suitability for factor analyses; the paper reports skewness between −0.66 and 0.79 and kurtosis between −0.30 and 0.25 as numerically comparable to the parent version. Average absolute skewness/kurtosis in an acceptable range supports ML estimation (per Muthén & Kaplan, 1985).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean comparisons between samples (t‑tests) with correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare means of English version to German construction sample using t‑tests and report significance with appropriate correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply multiple comparison correction (the paper used Bonferroni correction); interpret mean differences (e.g., English sample higher cheerfulness) and report sample sizes and t(df).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intercorrelations and convergent/discriminant evidence (Pearson correlations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute Pearson correlations between total scores and facets and examine patterns (homologous scales higher than heterologous; expected negative or positive associations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correlation patterns to assess convergent and discriminant validity (e.g., cheerfulness negatively correlates with seriousness and bad mood). Report significance levels and interpret in context of previous research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling adequacy: Kaiser‑Meyer‑Olkin (KMO) and Bartlett's sphericity
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess sample adequacy for factor analysis via KMO and Bartlett's test of sphericity (e.g., KMO = 0.93; Bartlett χ2 significant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High KMO (close to 1) and significant Bartlett's test indicate suitability for factor analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor retention criteria: eigenvalues (>1), scree test, and parallel analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide number of factors to retain using multiple criteria: eigenvalues >1, inspection of Scree plot, and parallel analysis comparing observed eigenvalues to those from randomly generated datasets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parallel analysis used here (100 random datasets) — retain factors whose eigenvalues exceed the random-data mean (upper 95th percentile). The paper retained three factors based on these combined criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor extraction method (principal axis factoring / exploratory factor analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an appropriate extraction method for facet/item intercorrelations (the paper used principal axis factoring (PAF) for facets and exploratory factor analysis in MPlus for items).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose extraction method consistent with data properties (e.g., PAF for facet intercorrelations; in MPlus use robust estimators for ordinal items).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rotation: use oblique rotation when factors are correlated
rubrics_metrics.description: If factors are not orthogonal, perform oblique rotation (the paper used oblique rotation/Oblimin).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oblique rotation allows factors to correlate and is appropriate when inter-factor correlations indicate non‑orthogonality. Report rotated loadings and interpret factor structure accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item and facet loadings and communalities (h2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Report factor loadings (items/facets should load highest on their theoretically expected factor) and communalities (h2) to indicate shared variance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List loadings (the paper reported all listed loadings > 0.20); use loading magnitudes to judge precision with which facets/items measure factors. Communality h2 indicates proportion of variance accounted for by factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross‑loadings / secondary loadings handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and allow for theoretically meaningful second loadings (e.g., CH1 and CH3 on BM; SE6 on CH; BM3 and BM5 on CH).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider models that permit specific secondary loadings when theory and data indicate cross‑loadings; report and interpret direction and magnitude (including negative second loadings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) approach and estimation
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform CFA (the paper used ML estimation in AMOS for facet-level CFA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of estimator assumptions (ML assumes continuous and normally distributed indicators); for ordinal Likert items consider alternative estimators (see WLSMV guidance). Report model comparisons and CFA fit indices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goodness‑of‑fit indices and cutoff interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use multiple fit indices (chi‑square, RMSEA, SRMR, NFI, Tucker‑Lewis/TL, CFI) and interpret with published cutoffs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chi‑square is sensitive to large N. The paper treats NFI and TL > 0.90 as indicators of acceptable fit and >0.95 as good; RMSEA and SRMR < 0.10 acceptable and < 0.05 good (citing Bollen & Long; Browne & Cudeck; Hu & Bentler). Use a multifaceted approach to judge model fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of Likert (ordinal) data: estimator and polychoric correlations
rubrics_metrics.description: For four‑point Likert items, consider treating responses as continuous with caution or use ordinal methods; the paper used exploratory factor analysis in MPlus with WLSMV estimator and polychoric correlations for the STCI‑T <60>.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WLSMV with polychoric correlations is recommended for ordinal items; ML on continuous covariance may require strong assumptions and very large N. Choose estimator appropriate to item format and sample size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample size requirements for factor analysis/CFA
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that confirmatory analyses of item‑level models require very large samples (especially with >20 items); the paper notes N > 20 items requires large N for accurate results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan independent large replication samples for CFA of short forms; the authors recommend validating the STCI‑T <60> in an independently collected sample with sufficient N to perform CFA reliably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item selection criteria for short form construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit criteria applied for deriving STCI‑T <60>: (a) best CITC with the own scale, (b) consider item content to preserve content domains, (c) balanced representation of facets (core facets get more weight if balance impossible), (d) avoid items with similar content or linguistic usage, (e) good convergence with item content of the German version (prefer paralleled items when similar), (f) 20 items per scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a concept‑guided strategy in item reduction rather than a purely empirical selection; consider indices from PAF and item analyses but preserve content validity and facet coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model comparison and selection across alternative theoretical models
rubrics_metrics.description: Test multiple theoretically plausible models (the paper tested six: one‑factor up to three‑factor with secondary loadings) and compare fit indices to select the best fitting model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report fit for each model (chi‑square, RMSEA, SRMR, NFI, TL) and interpret relative improvements; pick model balancing theory and acceptable fit (Model 6 chosen here despite not being exceptionally good).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspection of residuals and modification indices to refine model fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine residuals and modification indices; allow correlated residuals where theoretically justified (e.g., among facets forming each factor) to improve fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use modification indices cautiously and only when justified by theory/previous findings; report which residual correlations would improve fit and reason for allowing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replication across samples and multimethod evidence (self vs peer reports)
rubrics_metrics.description: Replicate scale characteristics (means, SDs, α, CITC) in independent/replication samples and across methods (self-report and peer‑report).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare self vs peer means and correlations (the paper reports no significant mean differences and moderate‑to‑good convergence, e.g., r = 0.74 for CH). Use replication to support external validity and convergence evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical/diagnostic recommendations based on psychometric results
rubrics_metrics.description: Advise users on appropriate uses of scales given psychometric properties (e.g., do not suggest facets for diagnostic purposes when facet reliabilities are low; refer to total scores which show high reliabilities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use total scores for research and diagnostic inferences if facet reliabilities are insufficient; further research needed for facet reliability across broader/older samples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation and cross‑national validation considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss translation methodology and the need to test instrument across nations (the translation deviated from classical back‑translation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Future studies should validate translations with classical procedures (e.g., back‑translation) and across different English‑speaking nations to assess generalizability and measurement invariance.
